historical_timeline.summary: Born in Cresson, Pennsylvania; his father dies within three years and his mother raises him in Maine.
Graduates from Bowdoin College as a civil engineer; later joins the Navy Civil Engineer Corps and hires Matthew Henson in Nicaragua.
First of eight Arctic expeditions, carried out with the help of Inughuit men and women.
Breaks both bones of a leg above the ankle aboard the Kite.
Brings six Inughuit people to New York; four die within months.
Both feet frozen on reaching Fort Conger, Ellesmere Island; most of his toes amputated in March.
Has two sons with an Inughuit woman in Greenland during the expeditions of these years.
Reports reaching the North Pole with Matthew Henson and four Inughuit men; the claim is disputed.
Retires as a rear admiral; lives in Washington, D.C., with summers on Eagle Island, Maine.
Dies of pernicious anemia; buried at Arlington National Cemetery. Liver therapy, the first effective treatment, came only after his death.

claims.statement: Robert Edwin Peary was born on May 6, 1856, in Cresson, Pennsylvania. His father died within three years of his birth, and his mother raised him in southern Maine.

claims.statement: He graduated from Bowdoin College as a civil engineer in 1877, joined the Coast and Geodetic Survey in Washington in 1879 and the U.S. Navy Civil Engineer Corps in 1881, and surveyed in Nicaragua for a proposed canal; there he hired Matthew Henson, the African American who proved indispensable to his Arctic work.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors his background as an engineer and naval officer.

source_links.locator: Class of 1877; Coast and Geodetic Survey 1879; Civil Engineers Corps 1881; hired Matthew Henson

claims.statement: From 1886 to 1909 he planned and led eight Arctic expeditions, one of them four years long, relying on the help of Inughuit (Polar Inuit) men and women of northwestern Greenland, who hunted, sledged, sewed and overwintered with his parties. On the 1891 to 1892 expedition he showed that Greenland is an island.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History of his work and of the Inughuit people whose labor made the expeditions possible; no health fact about any of them is recorded.

source_links.locator: eight arctic expeditions; a small group relying on Eskimo assistance
the Inughuit men and women who overwintered with them at Fort Conger
established the northern limit and insularity of Greenland

claims.statement: On July 11, 1891, aboard the Kite in the ice of Melville Bay, the iron tiller, jammed over by an ice cake, caught his leg against the deckhouse and broke both bones just above the ankle; the leg was set and he was carried ashore at the winter camp.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Past injury; the healed fracture is recorded in the past medical history.

source_links.locator: 1891 Melville Bay: A Broken Leg

claims.statement: In 1897, at the request of staff of the American Museum of Natural History, who had asked for one Inughuit man to work with the museum for a year, he brought six Inughuit people from Greenland to New York: three men, a woman and two children. Within months four of them had died; a boy of about seven, whose father was among the dead, was left an orphan far from home, and the museum kept his father's bones instead of burying them.
claims.clinical_interpretation: A documented part of his treatment of Inuit people, recorded plainly. It has no clinical role in the modern episode; no health fact about any of the six is recorded.

source_links.locator: six people made the trip; within months Qissuk and three of the others had died; his father's body processed by museum staff

claims.statement: On the expedition of 1898 to 1902, reaching the old station at Fort Conger on Ellesmere Island at midnight on January 6, 1899, he found that both feet were frozen; in March a doctor amputated the affected toes. He lost most of his toes, and the stumps were often left bloody and aching by knocks against rough ice on later journeys.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Anchors the synthetic toe amputations, the forefoot care and the importance of foot protection in the modern episode.

claims.statement: He married in 1888 and had two children with his wife. He also had two sons with an Inughuit woman in Greenland, born during his expeditions; his daughter's papers name them as her half-brothers, and one of them was an infant in the winter of 1900 to 1901.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented family history recorded plainly as history; no relative has any statement, decision or health fact in the modern episode, and no descendant is named.

claims.statement: On April 6, 1909, he reported reaching the North Pole with Matthew Henson and four Inughuit men, Ootah, Egingwah, Seegloo and Ooqueah (Odaq, Iggianguaq, Sigluk and Ukkujaaq in today's spelling). Frederick Cook announced a competing claim days before Peary returned; most geographic bodies came to credit Peary, but the claim has long been disputed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: History of his work and of his companions; the dispute is a documented fact, not a health fact.

claims.statement: He retired from the Navy in 1911 as a rear admiral with the Thanks of Congress, and lived his last years with his family in Washington, D.C., spending summers on Eagle Island on the Maine coast; the dispute over his claim cast a pall over those years.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Pernicious anemia in an older man with old frostbite amputations: a 62-year-old retired naval officer and polar explorer comes in with four months of fatigue, breathlessness, pallor, a sore tongue and numb, unsteady feet. The episode covers the blood count, MCV, smear and reticulocytes; vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, homocysteine and folate; iron studies; intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies and gastrin; treatment without delay when nerves are affected, with intramuscular cyanocobalamin loading, a weekly phase and lifelong monthly maintenance under the 2014 British Society for Haematology guideline and the 2024 NICE guideline, and high-dose oral therapy as an alternative; the reticulocyte response and the risk of low potassium early in treatment; restrictive transfusion; upper endoscopy for neuroendocrine tumors and gastric cancer risk and its surveillance under the 2021 AGA clinical practice update on atrophic gastritis; screening for autoimmune thyroid disease and diabetes; iron deficiency unmasked by recovery; the examination of subacute combined degeneration and its partial recovery; neuropathy and falls; and foot care for a man with old toe amputations, with footwear, daily skin checks and podiatry.

assessment.assessment: Confirmed. Severe cobalamin deficiency (a low vitamin B12 with a high methylmalonic acid) with megaloblastic pancytopenia and ineffective red cell production, and a positive intrinsic factor antibody, which is highly specific for pernicious anemia; a positive parietal cell antibody and a high gastrin show autoimmune loss of the acid-producing cells of the stomach. The samples were drawn after four injections; the laboratory's guidance on its intrinsic factor assay was followed, and the parietal cell antibody and gastrin agree. Folate is normal, and there is no dietary, drug or surgical cause

With neurological involvement, intramuscular treatment without delay is right. Complete the seven loading doses, then give 1,000 micrograms weekly while the nerves are improving, then monthly for life, because autoimmune gastritis does not recover. High-dose oral cyanocobalamin (at least 1 mg a day) works because about 1 percent of a large dose is absorbed without intrinsic factor, and is a reasonable maintenance alternative once he has recovered, if he prefers it and takes it reliably; NICE advises intramuscular treatment for life when autoimmune gastritis is the cause. Vitamin B12 levels need not be rechecked once treatment is established

No transfusion: he is stable at rest, the reticulocyte peak shows the marrow responding, and transfusion in severe megaloblastic anemia can overload the circulation. Potassium can fall in the first days of treatment as new cells take it up; the early check was missed, and today's 3.6 mmol/L is acceptable, to be repeated at the next visit. Iron deficiency often appears as the count recovers, because new cells use the stores and an acid-poor stomach absorbs iron poorly; iron studies should be repeated at about eight weeks

Upper endoscopy is advised now, with biopsies from the antrum, incisura and body in separate jars (updated Sydney protocol), to confirm autoimmune gastritis and to look for type 1 neuroendocrine tumors and dysplasia. Surveillance afterwards depends on the findings: endoscopy every one to two years if neuroendocrine tumors are found and removed; otherwise an interval decided with him, for example three years with extensive atrophy or metaplasia. A screening colonoscopy, never done, can be done at the same session

The posterior column and peripheral nerve signs fit subacute combined degeneration. Most recovery happens over three to six months and some numbness may remain, especially at the ends of the feet, so his old toe amputations and the new sensory loss together call for careful foot protection and balance training. Autoimmune thyroid disease is common with autoimmune gastritis: TSH is normal and the thyroid antibody negative; check TSH yearly. HbA1c is normal
